title: Kernel hiccup synthesis and mitigation notes
content:
Purpose:
Quick synthesis notebook for the set of small, repeatable kernel-level interruptions we've been seeing across the fleet (quiet, short-duration 'hiccups' rather than full panics). Goal is to capture signals, attempted mitigations, and a short experiment plan to reduce customer-facing tail latencies.

One-line summary:
- Since late November we've observed ~0.5–1.5% of requests hitting transient kernel-scheduler stalls on a subset of DGX-like nodes. Symptoms: single-request stalls (5–30s) with later automatic recovery, increased correctable ECC counts on the same host in preceding 30m. NVLink peer resets sometimes observed within the same 5m window. Not a wholesale driver crash, but a soft instability that's increasing tail latency and triggering evictions.

Impact and customer observations:
- Affected jobs: long-context chat sessions and some batched generation routes.
- External: a handful of Hosted API 95/99th latency spikes reported (linked Slack thread). No data loss or models corrupted.
- Internal: autoscaler evictions spike for the affected hostclass, causing burst routing to fallback pools.

What we saw (raw signals):
- Telemetry: correctable ECC counts increased from baseline 0–2/hour to 20–80/hour in 30–60m leading up to the stall windows.
- dmesg snippets (anonymized):
  [kernel] NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:65:00): 79, 0x00000000
  [kernel] nvlink: peer-reset detected on link 2
  [kernel] GPU ECC single-bit corrected (device 0000:65:00)
- nvml query: process list empty at time of stall; GPU utilization ~2–5% (mostly idle) immediately after stall.
- kworker stacks: kworker/7:2 blocked for 19s waiting for irq/PCIe completion on the host.

Quick reproduction notes (lab):
- Synthetic load: running sustained mem-intensive workloads + intermittent NVLink peer streaming reproduces modest ECC spike but not always the stall.
- Correlation is strongest when system firmware (BMC) firmware is on older rev and GPUs are at a particular microcode (v4.2.1). We've seen reproduction in lab when mixing older BMC + v4.2.1 GPUs.

Root-candidate hypotheses (ranked):
1) NVLink link retraining causing momentary PCIe transaction stall cascades to kernel worker threads. Correctable ECCs are a symptom, link retraining is the cause.
2) Driver microcode/path with memory scrub scheduling interaction — when scrub occurs during heavy kernel timestamp operations, we see kworker stalls.
3) PSU-level voltage jitter causing ecc bursts which provoke low-level driver state transitions and temporary firmware-level resets. Less likely but not impossible (some hosts co-located with older PSUs).
4) Telemetry sampling artifact (false positive) — some of the stalls are induced by our heavy polling from the telemetry agent itself. (Action: quick disable agent on a single host to check.)

Mitigations we've tried (and results):
- Soft restart of nvidia modules (modprobe -r && modprobe nvidia): often clears the condition but is disruptive (kills local containers).
- Blacklisting noisy GPU in the scheduler (manual): reduces customer impact but is a manual process and hides root cause.
- Bumping ECC scrub interval down (less frequent): reduced ECC bursts in one lab run but did not remove stalls.
- Rolling forward GPU microcode to v4.3.0 (canary hosts): reduced frequency on canary from 1%->0.2% over 72h. Encouraging but limited sample size.
- Telemetry agent throttle: disabling polling on one host removed a couple of short stalls across 48h — suggests telemetry noise could be amplifying in-host contention.

Short experiment plan (72–168h window):
- Experiment A: Canary group (4 nodes) with microcode v4.3.0 + BMC fw latest + telemetry agent sampling doubled interval. Monitor below: correctable ECC rate, kernel kworker stall count, route tail latency. If 50% drop across all metrics -> plan broader rollout. (Owner: Lena)
- Experiment B: One host with telemetry agent disabled + repeat same batched/generation workload to see if stalls still occur. If stalls persist -> telemetry not cause. (Owner: Priya)
- Experiment C: GPU power-capping (limit to 85% via nvidia-smi) for a window to rule out PSU voltage jitter. Watch for ECC changes + stalls. (Owner: Marcus)

Monitoring / Alerts to add (short list):
- Add a kworker stall metric: sample stack state and increment a "kworker-stall" counter when any worker blocked >5s.
- Correlate nvlink peer-reset events with correctable ECC burst windows in a join table.
- Temporary alert: if node correctable ECC > 20 in 30m AND nvlink peer-reset > 1 -> auto-quarantine.

Operational playbook (temp):
- If quarantine triggered -> shift traffic, mark node for next maintenance window, do a non-destructive nvml health check and collect full dmesg + nvlink logs.
- Avoid module unload on production hosts unless traffic can be drained (unload kills user containers). Prefer routing mitigation.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Can we get NVIDIA confirmation on v4.2.1 known nvlink retrain bug? (Opened support case: SR-128992)
- Is there a telemetry agent upgrade that reduces in-host contention? (Check agent v2.5 perf notes)
- Validate PSU voltage logs (ask infra to attach PSU health logs to the node for last 72h). Action: @infra-team.
- Run a longer (7d) canary with microcode + BMC combos to get stable numbers before fleet roll.

Notes to self (informal):
- Don't escalate to full fleet rollback without 3-day canary. We nearly rolled drivers prematurely in December and that caused cluster-wide flakiness.
- Keep the SRE rotation in the loop; nightly triage has been useful for catching recurrence pattern.

Appendix / useful commands (for oncall):
- collect quick stack: sudo journalctl -k -b -1 --no-pager | tail -n 200 > /tmp/kstack.log
- nvml dump: sudo python3 /usr/local/bin/nvml-dump.py --full > /tmp/nvml.json
- check ECC: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.ecc.errors.uncorrected.volatile,memory.ecc.errors.corrected.volatile --format=csv

References / links:
- JIRA: SRE-8723 (primary incident), SRE-8799 (telemetry agent perf investigation)
- PR: runtime PR #1291 (microcode rollout automation)
- Slack: #sre-ops thread: thread-xyZ123 (customer reports and quick triage notes)

If you read nothing else: prioritise the microcode canary + telemetry-agent throttle experiment. If both reduce rate materially we can schedule a controlled microcode rollout with rollback hooks.
